_comment: Plain-language replacements for authored project text, applied by proj_lib.dump. Keys are project ids; each maps a field to its new value, or {"old": ..., "new": ...} pairs for list fields. The build fails if an old value is not found.

pj.p00.1.why: Breaking things on purpose, with nothing at stake, shows you can recover with Git.

pj.p01.1.why: Uses most of the phase (input, data structures, files, errors) with no libraries.

requirements.old: Reject bad input with a clear message rather than a traceback.
requirements.new: Reject bad input with a clear message instead of a traceback.

pj.p01.2.why: Moving the rules from if-statements into a dictionary separates data from logic.

pj.p02.1.why: Memory has to stay flat, which only generators give you.

stretch.old: Parallelise the aggregation and measure whether it actually helps.
stretch.new: Parallelise the aggregation and measure whether it helps.

pj.p02.2.title: A small library that implements protocols
pj.p02.2.brief: A reusable package that implements the iterator, context manager and descriptor protocols instead of only using them.
pj.p02.2.why: Implementing the protocols shows how Python's data model works.

pj.p03.1.why: Makes your code installable by other people, not just runnable on your machine.

pj.p04.1.why: Building each structure once shows its trade-offs.

requirements.old: At least one structure where your version loses, and an honest explanation.
requirements.new: At least one structure where your version loses, and why.

pj.p05.1.why: Writing down your reasoning is what carries over to new problems.

pj.p06.1.why: Exit codes let monitoring systems trust your automation.

pj.p07.1.why: Seeing the raw bytes makes every higher layer easier to debug.

pj.p08.1.why: Index tuning only shows its effect with enough data.

pj.p09.1.why: The closest match to a backend job. It needs to be complete.

pj.p10.1.why: It must handle network, site and machine failures, not just the happy path.

pj.p11.1.brief: The same workload implemented four ways, and measured.
pj.p11.1.why: Shows which concurrency model suits which workload, with measurements.

pj.p12.1.why: Someone new can run it from the README alone.

pj.p13.1.why: Finding a flaw in your own code teaches more than reading about it.

pj.p14.1.brief: Train something small, then spend most of the effort measuring whether it works.
pj.p14.1.why: Evaluation is the hard part. Measure whether the model works.

pj.p14.2.why: Writing the chain rule yourself and checking it numerically shows how autograd works.

pj.p16.1.brief: Read the bytecode, measure the memory, and write a native extension that is worth its complexity.

requirements.old: Write one extension in C, Cython or Rust and benchmark it honestly.
requirements.new: Write one extension in C, Cython or Rust and benchmark it against the Python version.

pj.p17.1.why: A pipeline you can re-run is a pipeline you can fix.

pj.p99.1.brief: Build, release and maintain something other people use.
pj.p99.1.why: Real users, bug reports and maintenance.

requirements.old: A README good enough that nobody has to ask you how to start.
requirements.new: A README that explains how to start.
